item.title: Emergency Alert System for 15,000 Users: LLM, PostGIS, Qdrant, and Telegram
item.description:
The main engineering challenge here is to transform a stream of unstructured text from hundreds of Telegram channels into events that the rest of the system can work with: determine the event type, location, brief description, remove duplicates, and understand who exactly needs to receive it. We initially built the system without constant manual moderation. Events appear around the clock, so manual verification doesn't scale well. Part of the work is done by an LLM pipeline, and part by users who can report events themselves and verify each other's messages. Read more

item.title: Eleven Releases in a Day: How We Fixed an AI Agent's Memory and What Came of It
item.description:
I sat down to test my own tool — local memory for code agents — and found eleven things that needed fixing. A stop hook that recursively spawned 4083 sessions in a day; recall that was dead on a standard installation; migration taking 66 seconds within a hook with a 10-second timeout. A breakdown of each item: what broke, how we fixed it, and who found it — me, an external review by another model, CI, or testing on a live Ubuntu. Read on

item.title: Vibe Coding Until the First Catastrophe: Isolating AI Agents
item.description:
The IT industry was recently shaken by an autonomous AI agent running on Claude that destroyed a company's production database in 9 seconds, despite explicit instructions not to. This incident, along with others like Replit's AI agent deleting a database and Claude Engineer deleting .git and ~/.ssh, highlights the dangers of giving AI agents unrestricted access to your system. The article discusses the mechanics of these catastrophes, emphasizing that soft guardrails like system prompts are insufficient. It introduces Agent Bunker, an open-source tool that creates isolated environments (sandboxes) for AI agents, preventing them from harming the host system or accessing sensitive data. The article concludes by stressing the importance of using such isolation tools as a necessary developer hygiene measure in the age of AI agents.

item.title: Part 3. Silicon hacked silicon, or how I became the author of the world's first confirmed PCIe GEN2 X16 for CMP90HX
item.description:
This is already the third major series of provocations against the NVIDIA CMP 90HX, where we will bypass another limitation imposed by NVIDIA. In the first article, I assembled a home server with a bunch of former mining cards. In the second article, I delved into the driver, figured out the V67 mechanism, and through the service part of the GPU, reached the computational limitations of the CMP 90HX. It turned out that a large part of the computational power was hidden from me. We brought it back. At this point, a good server owner would probably thank the hardware for its work and start using it. But the ability to stop in time was not installed in this server when I assembled it... Read more

item.title: I Inserted a Contract into ChatGPT - What Did I Violate? An Analysis of Federal Law No. 152 with Figures and Cases
item.description:
Many articles about neural networks and Federal Law No. 152 state that a company faces a fine of 20,000 rubles for sending a contract with third-party personal data to ChatGPT. This figure comes from an old version of the Code of Administrative Offenses and applies to an official, not a company. Since May 2025, legal entities face fines of 150,000-300,000 rubles. I delved into the law's text, Roskomnadzor's figures, and court cases. I found one Russian case involving a neural network, related to labor law, not personal data. In it, the court stated a crucial point that everyone needs to accept: sending a document to a neural network is equivalent to transferring it to a third party. I will further explain what violates the law when a contract is inserted into ChatGPT, what does not, and why the 15 million ruble figures in headlines are irrelevant.

item.title: How to Turn Habr from a Social Media Feed into a Library and Knowledge Base
item.description:
Habr presents content as a social media feed: readers primarily engage with new posts and discussions, and after a couple of weeks, an article fades from view. It might resurface if external search engines or users from other platforms link to it. The feed favors frequent and voluminous publications. However, over 20 years, the platform has accumulated a rare knowledge base: some old articles still answer current questions, are saved in bookmarks, and their topics remain relevant for decades. I understand that every project needs to survive and profit. To Habr's credit, readers can focus on content without distracting ads and banners! But this advantage also has a downside: advertising becomes less overt and is woven into the text. You start reading an article and find links to Telegram channels from independent authors urging subscriptions. Corporate blogs recommend hosting virtual machines, AI chatbot aggregators, doses of "neuro-slop" for SEO, promoting company HR brands to create candidate queues, and so on. This situation is unlikely to improve. Moderation and platform policies won't save readers. The balance between the commercial interests of selling corporate subscriptions and motivating independent, unpaid enthusiast authors to create and publish useful material is disrupted. When a technical article, which you spent days writing, is pushed out of the feed by superficial materials generated faster than Fibonacci rabbits, created solely for brand promotion. The author can't find their audience, and anything beyond the second or third page of the feed is unlikely to be seen by anyone, except for a small chance of being discovered through Google or Yandex search results. I'm not advocating against "bees for honey"! But I will offer my approach, which allows searching for needed information among tens and hundreds of thousands of articles. Habr has content of the highest quality: descriptions of solutions to practical problems, frameworks, technologies, features, and programming language constructs, how to survive in a corporation or startup. All of this can be found by both humans and automated agents; all that's needed is to process and prepare this information array. And yes, neural networks and clustering algorithms are used here to process articles and group them. We will group 34,000 Habr articles by meaning and catalog them, reading similar topics without trusting the keywords and hubs indicated by the author. Similarly, you can create your own local knowledge base from personal materials and notes at work and home, without sharing this information with cloud API services of neural networks if you wish. This structured information will be much easier for an AI agent to find for solving your technical tasks that require precise solutions, algorithms, and "recipes." The material in the article, not hidden under a spoiler, is written manually using the old-fashioned "tube" method. Read more

item.description:
Vault Audit AI has evolved from an Obsidian note auditing plugin into a system with a separate Companion, MCP access for AI clients, and secure change proposals. I explain why the project was split into two repositories, why agents cannot directly write to the Vault, how the self-hosted Companion works, and why all this led to a rebranding to Veynrel. item.title: I wanted to build an app, but ended up managing a department of AI agents
item.description:
On August 31st, my app's production environment was down for about an hour. The reason was embarrassingly simple. An agent added all files from a shared working folder to a commit, including someone else's unfinished work. Then it did it again. The second time, after it had just written rules stating this shouldn't be done. Then it started fixing things. An error, a fix, another error, another fix. Each fix caused a new problem. I looked at it and typed: 'just revert to the old version.' Meaning, roll back to the last state known to be working. And then I caught myself having a strange feeling. I had just conducted an incident review. Exactly as I had done for years at work with live teams. The thought that had been swirling in my mind since June finally clicked that evening: I'm not building an app with AI. I'm managing a department. Read more

item.title: Review of the book "Designing Large Language Model Applications"
item.description:
The book "Designing Large Language Model Applications" by Suhas Pai aims to help developers bridge the gap between calling a language model API and building a truly functional and market-competitive product application. The book examines LLMs as a component of a complex system, from the transformer architecture to RAG pipelines and agents. For a developer or ML engineer who has already moved past the initial prototype stage, this is a valuable resource that breaks down LLM application architecture step-by-step, without reducing the material to a mere list of prompts. Read more

item.title: ChatGPT Business for a Russian Team in 2026: Tariffs, Corporate Payment, Documents
item.description:
ChatGPT Business is OpenAI's team plan: shared workspace, admin panel, SSO, and a contractual guarantee that employee conversations won't be used for model training. It's not sold directly to Russian legal entities because OpenAI only accepts card payments, and Russian bank cards are rejected. We cover the current 2026 tariffs, how Business differs from Plus, and how to pay for it as a company with a full set of documents in 1 business day.

item.title: How We Change Models in the Developer Agent
item.description:
A new language model can appear in the morning, be at the top of several leaderboards by evening, and be replaced by the next version in a couple of weeks. For a team using LLMs in a product, this raises the question: when to update and how to do it without undue risk to users and development. At Pervaya Forma, an AI agent assists in the development pipeline: it works with code, tools, and reviews. We regularly review the set of models in this pipeline. In recent weeks, we updated Muse Spark from version 1.2 to 1.3, added Gemini 3.8 Flash, and prepared a quick rollback for it to the previous model. We will explain how this process works. Read more

item.title: Can a Working Interface Be Built with AI in an Hour?
item.description:
"I'll just throw a prompt into AI, and in a second I'll get a ready-made interface, my own website, or a dashboard" — this idea has surely crossed the mind of anyone not involved in design or development. AI tools for these fields are actively spreading and promise such fantastic results that the thought arises: what if designers will soon be unnecessary? After all, there is a big gap between a picture and a working prototype. Hierarchy of elements on the screen, adaptability, accessibility, scenario logic, and product metrics are just a limited list of points that are very difficult to fit into a single prompt. I forgot to introduce myself: my name is Kamila, I am an interface designer at Selectel. Along with the AI boom, colleagues have started coming to me more often with questions like: "The AI made me a mockup, please review it." So I decided to figure it out from my design perspective — where AI can help, and where it creates an attractive, but not very functional concept. Read more

item.title: How I Built a Room Security Guard with YOLO and Connected it to Telegram
item.description:
I live alone and usually know who might be at my home. But when I'm away, unpleasant thoughts sometimes creep in. 'What if someone did come in while I was gone?' It could have been a neighbor, a relative, or a repairman, but without a camera, you can only guess. I wanted to solve this with a simple script. The camera sees a person at the door, and a message and a frame arrive in Telegram. I got a bit carried away in the process. The result is a bot with support for multiple cameras, alerts, voice, facial recognition, and the ability to offload data processing to a separate server. In this article, I'll explain why YOLO is needed here and why a simple motion detector wasn't enough. How I tested the project's functionality in real conditions, why I don't send regular photos of people to the chat, and how privacy is organized. Also, how to connect a phone as a camera and offload heavy processing to a remote server. Read on.

item.title: How China is Developing AI, Energy, and Data Centers: Facts and a Comparison with xAI as an Example
item.description:
In China's Inner Mongolia, computing power requiring gigawatts of electricity is being planned. Nearby, wind and solar farms, storage, substations, and communication lines are being built. In Memphis, USA, xAI accelerated the launch of Colossus using an existing industrial building and its own gas generation. Both stories share a common engineering challenge: servers can be purchased faster than everything needed for their continuous operation can be prepared. Read more
